newsitem.title: ROMANIA: BULL RUN PUSHES MOST EAST EURO STOCKS HIGHER.
newsitem.headline: BULL RUN PUSHES MOST EAST EURO STOCKS HIGHER.

text.p: A strong bull run brought a flying start for most East European stocks in the first week of trading this year with Warsaw hitting record highs and prices soaring in Prague and Ljubliana.
Budapest's bullish trend was capped down by profit-taking on Friday, with Warsaw expecting a similar move next week.
Bratislava shifted to higher gear and shares in Zagreb and Bucharest were on the rise. Tirana had no trades and Bulgaria stock trading remained suspended.
WARSAW
Polish shares surged this week, setting three consecutive 33-month highs but analysts were not sure whether the rally would continue next week.
They said profit-taking was likely early next week, but were unsure whether the market, buoyed by foreign buying, would hit new records or fall later in the week.
The WIG index soared 6.4 percent this week to 15,418.9 points.

"I don't think the trend will last on the long term. It's too violent and seems to be purely psychological, not based on fundamentals. It's difficult to say when it will end," said Pawel Tarnowski of Raiffeisen Capital and Investment Polska.
Analysts said investors would be watching December and 1996 inflation data due on Wednesday, as the central bank said a possible decision to raise rates might hinge on those figures.
BUDAPEST
The Budapest Stock Exchange began the year in an euphoric mood with the BUX index steadily climbing from last December's rally despite Friday's 10.09 drop amid profit-taking.

The BUX hit the 14th successive record high in a row on Thursday, closing at 4,724.59 points, up 161.76. The BUX has more than tripled since the beginning of 1996 and rose 14 percent from December 31.

Traders said the bull run was driven by fresh interest of foreign and domestic investors on a worldwide rising trend on stock markets. Good Hungarian macroeconomic figures and corporate results also underpinned investors sentiment that Hungarian shares were undervalued.
The pace of the rally took traders by surprise. Even though a downwards correction may come any time, they said Hungarian stocks were likely to extend their gains substantially in 1997.
PRAGUE

Czech shares took off with gains this year and analysts say foreign investors may be diverting their attention to the relatively undervalued PX50 after realising strong gains last year in Warsaw and Budapest.
"We cannot expect the same strong interest in Poland and Hungary so the investors have decided to put money into the Czech Republic," said Miroslav Nosal of Patria Finance.

Last year the PX50 index rose by just 27 percent compared with well over 100 percent in Budapest and nearly 90 percent in Warsaw. In the week to Friday, the PX50 rose 3.4 percent to 557.8 powered by strong performances from major issues.
BRATISLAVA
Trading on the Bratislava Stock Exchange opened listless this week, but brokers said they expected activity to pick up, boosted mainly by foreign investors.
They said demand for blue chips and reluctance to sell at the currently prices may underpin the upward trend.
The 12-share SAX index rose 1.42 points to close at 179.47 on Friday.
LJUBLJANA
Slovenian shares this week jumped 8.88 percent. The ten-share SBI index rose 105.3 points to 1,290.5.
Health resort Terme Catez operator was the biggest gainer, while warehouse BTC was the leading decliner.
BUCHAREST

Most Bucharest bourse shares drifted higher this week, with turnover climbing to 70 million lei on Tuesday before sinking to a quarter of that level on Thursday amid thin trading interest, brokers said.
Fertiliser-maker Azomures SA stayed in the limelight, gaining 1,200 lei on Thursday to close at 14,300.
Two unofficial indices - the VAB, computed by Vanguard SA and Bucharest Investment Group's BIG -- rose by 2.9 percent and 2.72 percent from the previous session.
ZAGREB
Croatian stocks closed the week on a firmer note despite some losses on Friday when blue chips including fully listed drugs firm Pliva and Zagrebacka Banka kept the upward trend.
Pliva, the most actively traded issue on Friday, hit a new record gaining 35 kuna to 450, with 8,257 issues sold. Its GDR's in London also hit a new $16.56 high.

All eyes are set on the credit rating Croatia is expected to get next week, when three leading rating agencies are to announce their assessment. It is widely expected to be solid and should help prop up prices of all liquid stocks.
TIRANA
Albania's fledgling Tirana Stock Exchange started the year with two eventless sessions on Monday and Thursday.
"Everybody was in a selling mood because they seemed to need liquidity but no deals were struck," a broker said.
The eight-month-old exchange trades in 364-day government treasury bills, bonds and privatisation vouchers. JAN 10
